questions.question: A coach wants swimmers to develop controlled aerobic endurance. What should determine the design of the set?
options: The number of metres normally used by the squad.
The intended response, followed by suitable pace, repetitions, recovery and technical focus.
The interval that allows the fastest swimmer to complete the most repetitions.
The training category written beside the set.
questions.explanation: Begin with the objective; the planned distance or label does not by itself establish the demand.

questions.question: Two swimmers complete 8 × 100 m on the same send-off. One reports 4/10 effort with stable technique; the other 8/10 with deteriorating control. What does this demonstrate?
options: The second swimmer necessarily trained more effectively.
The same written set can create different demands and require individual adjustments.
A common send-off guarantees equal recovery and adaptation.
The first swimmer should always increase distance.
questions.explanation: Swim times, available rest, effort and technique determine the response.

questions.question: Why is actual recovery important when evaluating a repeated set?
options: It establishes time before the next repetition and changes the demand of subsequent work.
It remains unchanged whenever the send-off is fixed.
It only matters for maximum speed.
It is more useful than all other observations combined.
questions.explanation: A fixed interval can provide progressively less rest as swim times slow.

questions.question: A coach writes 3 × 400 m and labels it EN1. Which observation supports that objective?
options: The swimmer finishes even at near-maximal effort.
The swimmer holds sustainable effort, controlled breathing and stable technique.
The swimmer gets the longest possible rest.
The distance alone confirms EN1.
questions.explanation: The intended controlled aerobic demand must be confirmed from the swimmer's response.

questions.question: Why is substantial recovery suitable for repeated maximum-speed efforts?
options: It allows fatigue to accumulate as fast as possible.
It protects peak velocity and coordination across repetitions.
It guarantees aerobic improvement.
It removes the need to monitor technique.
questions.explanation: Pure speed training prioritises very fast, technically coordinated efforts.

questions.question: Which distinction between the LP and LT examples is consistent with the lesson?
options: LP protects high output with substantial rest; LT uses deliberately incomplete rest in hard repeats.
They differ only by swimming distance.
LP always requires minimal rest.
LT requires full recovery after each repetition.
questions.explanation: The purpose of recovery distinguishes high-output and deliberately fatiguing sets.

questions.question: The swimmer meets the 100 m target three times but then slows. What should a coach investigate first?
options: Whether the total distance was finished.
Whether one faster repeat is possible.
Changes in technique, actual recovery, effort and earlier session work.
Whether everyone else also slowed.
questions.explanation: Slower times are an observation, not a sufficient explanation.

questions.question: Maximum-speed repetitions lose velocity and coordination. What best protects the objective?
options: Continue unchanged because fatigue is useful.
Shorten recovery to increase difficulty.
Extend rest, reduce repetitions or stop speed work when quality cannot recover.
Increase the distance to maintain volume.
questions.explanation: The speed objective is lost when very fast and technically sound work cannot be reproduced.

questions.question: The coach changes the send-off after repetition four. What should be recorded?
options: Only the total distance.
The original prescription and actual times, send-offs, completed repetitions and changes.
Only the new send-off, deleting the original.
Only the fastest repetition.
questions.explanation: Keep the planned prescription separate from the work actually delivered.

questions.question: A coach wants controlled endurance for swimmers with different abilities. Which approach best fits that objective?
options: Give everyone the same pace and send-off.
Individualise pace and rest where necessary to obtain similarly controlled responses.
Use the fastest athlete's pace for everyone.
Use longer repetitions for everyone.
questions.explanation: The coaching aim is an appropriate relative demand, not identical numbers.

questions.question: A swimmer completes 6 × 200 m at consistent times, but each feels near-maximal. The aim was sustainable aerobic work. What follows?
options: Consistent times prove success.
Effort suggests the intended sustainable demand may not have been achieved.
Relabel the session maximum speed.
Reduce the rest automatically.
questions.explanation: Repeatability alone does not establish whether effort and quality fitted the objective.

questions.question: A swimmer cannot reproduce the desired EN3 demand during 6 × 100 m. What should the coach consider?
options: Keep the target unchanged regardless of response.
Adjust pace, repetition length, recovery or volume to make demanding aerobic work appropriately repeatable.
Replace with easy work but keep the EN3 label.
Remove all recovery.
questions.explanation: Distances and recoveries are examples, not fixed definitions of EN3.

questions.question: Two swimmers complete similar 50 m times but one has less rest and deteriorating technique. What is supported?
options: Their demand must be identical.
The shorter recovery can create a different demand requiring evaluation against the objective.
Less rest always means better speed adaptation.
The swim time alone is sufficient.
questions.explanation: Technical execution and actual recovery affect the stimulus.

questions.question: During 4 × 50 m high-output work with substantial rest, performance declines sharply. Which response is most defensible?
options: Continue because severe fatigue is essential.
Check whether high output can be reproduced; adjust recovery or end the set if not.
Shorten rest automatically.
Treat the decline as EN1.
questions.explanation: The LP-oriented intention requires maintaining sufficiently high quality and output.

questions.question: During LT-oriented hard repeats, effort rises and times drift moderately while technique remains acceptable. How interpret this?
options: Any slowing is failure.
Some drift may fit the aim if quality and safety remain appropriate.
Always add repeats as effort rises.
Stop monitoring because fatigue was intended.
questions.explanation: Planned incomplete recovery can cause fatigue but must remain bounded.

questions.question: A swimmer completes all prescribed aerobic metres, but effort rises greatly and stroke control declines. What does volume alone establish?
options: Only that the distance was completed, not that the intended response occurred.
The intended adaptation was achieved.
Long-term capability improved.
The original prescription should be recorded as delivered unchanged.
questions.explanation: Actual work and observed response must be interpreted together.

questions.question: During 6 × 100 m on 1:50, three late repeats exceed target and stroke count and effort rise. What is the best decision?
options: Demand the original target without change.
Check the swimmer and modify the remaining work if needed to preserve the objective.
Delete the slower results.
Assume lack of aerobic capacity.
questions.explanation: The evidence suggests an objective/response mismatch requiring coaching judgement.

questions.question: One unusually fast training repetition is recorded. What can be said about development?
options: It proves lasting improvement.
It guarantees matching competition performance.
It is useful evidence, but long-term improvement needs repeated observations and context.
Other repetitions no longer matter.
questions.explanation: One performance cannot by itself prove durable adaptation.

questions.question: A set was modified because the swimmer could not maintain pace and technique. What review best informs future decisions?
options: Compare only completed metres.
Treat the original training label as proof of the adaptation.
Review the objective, actual splits, recovery, technique, modifications and patterns across sessions.
Use only the fastest repetition.
questions.explanation: Intent, observation, adjustment and accurate records form the central coaching process.
